# AI Coding Platforms Compared (Individual / Small-Team Lens, April 2026)

**Last revised:** 2026-04-26

## TL;DR

Six AI coding platforms — IBM Bob, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini (Code Assist + CLI + Antigravity), GitHub Copilot, Windsurf — span four fundamentally different deployment models (terminal CLI, IDE plugin, fork-IDE, enterprise platform). For an individual or small-team buyer in April 2026, the **headline finding is that pricing and product positioning shifted materially in the 11 days before this writing**: Windsurf 2.0 launched April 15 with embedded Devin [22][39], GitHub paused Copilot Pro/Pro+/Student signups April 20 [12][13], Anthropic silently moved Claude Code to Max-only on April 22 and reverted within hours [5], and GitHub's training-data policy for Free/Pro/Pro+ took effect April 24 [14]. Anyone using a comparison written before mid-April 2026 is reading from before this turbulence.

For most individual buyers in April 2026: **Claude Code on Pro $20/mo** is the strongest balance of model quality (Opus 4.7 leads SWE-bench Verified at 87.6% [32]) and surface flexibility (CLI + VS Code + JetBrains + Desktop + Web + iOS [2]). **Cursor on Pro $20/mo** is the strongest fork-IDE alternative if you want a single visual editor and Composer 2 (Cursor's own model) at $0.50/M input tokens [8]. **GitHub Copilot Pro $10/mo** has the broadest IDE coverage [15] but **cannot be signed up for new today** [12][13] and now uses your interaction data for training by default [14]. **Antigravity** is currently the cheapest path to Claude Opus 4.6 specifically, with Google subsidizing the access [19] — but with rate-limit reliability issues. **IBM Bob** at $20/mo + $3 support is genuinely accessible to individuals [26] but is built around RPG/COBOL/IBM i — outside that niche the product is a category mismatch. **Windsurf Pro $20/mo** with Devin Cloud sessions on Max is the agent-orchestration play.

The independent randomized productivity evidence remains uncomfortable: METR's 2025 RCT found AI tools made experienced developers **19% slower** while developers perceived themselves as 20% faster [34]. GitClear's repo analysis shows code duplication rising and refactoring rates falling across Google/Microsoft/Meta repos [35]. None of this should determine an individual buying decision, but it should set realistic expectations.

## What each thing actually is (disambiguation)

The user's prompt named "IBM Bob vs Claude Code vs Cursor vs Gemini" — these are different categories of thing. Comparing them as if they were interchangeable assumes they serve the same role. Here's what each actually is:

- **Claude Code** is Anthropic's agentic coding tool. Its canonical surface is a terminal CLI; it also ships VS Code and JetBrains plugins, a Desktop app, a web UI at `claude.ai/code`, and an iOS app, all backed by the same engine [2].
- **Cursor** is a standalone IDE that is a hard fork of VS Code, with Anysphere's AI features baked in. There is no Cursor extension you install into another editor; Cursor IS the editor [7].
- **Gemini** is three distinct products from Google: **Gemini Code Assist** (an IDE plugin) [17], **Gemini CLI** (an open-source terminal agent), and **Antigravity** (a separate fork-IDE in public preview since November 2025) [18]. Pricing and capability differ sharply across the three; this comparison treats them collectively because that's how the user named them but flags differences throughout.
- **GitHub Copilot** is a portfolio: extensions for 8+ IDEs (VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains, Neovim, Eclipse, Xcode, Azure Data Studio, Android Studio for Code Assist parity) [15], a CLI, a web "Workspace" planning tool, and a cloud "Coding Agent" that opens PRs from issue assignments.
- **Windsurf** is both a fork-IDE (Windsurf, formerly Codeium) and a 40+-IDE plugin set. Now owned by Cognition AI (makers of Devin) since the July 2025 acquisition [23]; Windsurf 2.0 (April 15, 2026) embeds Devin Cloud sessions [22][39].
- **IBM Bob** is two products under one name: **Bob-IDE** (a full fork of VS Code per [27]) and **Bob Shell** (a separate terminal CLI). GA'd March 24, 2026 [26]. Despite IBM's enterprise heritage, Bob is self-serve at $20/mo + $3 support — meaningfully accessible to individuals.

The framing implication: a fair comparison must normalize for what the buyer actually installs and runs. The deliverable below does that per dimension.

## Dimension 1: Deployment model

See [`references/deployment-model.md`](references/deployment-model.md). Summary: Claude Code wins on surface diversity (CLI + 4 IDEs + web + mobile) [2]. GitHub Copilot wins on IDE coverage breadth (8+) [15]. Cursor, Antigravity, Windsurf, Bob are each fork-IDEs — you commit to running their editor. Gemini Code Assist + Gemini CLI are the lighter-touch options.

## Dimension 2: Pricing and free tier

See [`references/pricing-and-free-tier.md`](references/pricing-and-free-tier.md). Headline finding: $20/mo is the entry price for serious individual use across **five** of the six platforms (Claude Code [1], Cursor [7], Antigravity AI Pro $19.99 [19], Windsurf [21], IBM Bob $20+$3 [26]). GitHub Copilot Pro is $10/mo — but **new Pro/Pro+ signups have been paused since April 20, 2026** [12][13][38]. The Cursor June 2025 pricing apology [10] and Anthropic's April 22 2026 silent pricing flip-flop [5] are reminders that pricing in this space is not stable; quote-of-the-day changes are common.

## Dimension 3: Models and flexibility

See [`references/models-and-flexibility.md`](references/models-and-flexibility.md). The "model layer" is increasingly commoditized — four of the six platforms (Cursor [7], GitHub Copilot [15], Antigravity [18], Windsurf [24]) expose Claude Opus/Sonnet directly. Cursor has its own frontier model (Composer 2 at $0.50/M input [8]). Windsurf has its SWE-1.6 family [24]. Antigravity is currently positioned in market terms as a "Claude Opus 4.6 access path" with Google subsidy [19]. **IBM Bob is the only platform where the user does not choose the model** — Bob auto-routes among Granite, Claude, Llama, Mistral. Differentiation is at the agent / context / IDE layer, not the model layer.

## Dimension 4: Agentic capabilities

See [`references/agentic-capabilities.md`](references/agentic-capabilities.md). All six platforms now support MCP. Claude Code's distinguishing feature is Skills (~30-50 tokens vs MCP's ~55K for a 5-server setup [6]) plus deterministic hooks [2]. Antigravity's Manager Surface is the most explicit multi-agent UX [18]. Windsurf 2.0's Devin handoff (plan locally, delegate to cloud) is the strongest hybrid local+cloud agent pattern [22][39]. GitHub Copilot Coding Agent (assign issue → get PR) is the strongest cloud-only agent. Bob's five modes (Ask / Plan / Code / Advanced / Orchestrator) are the most structured autonomy gradient. Cursor's agent has documented quality regressions in the 2.x era [11].

## Dimension 5: Context and codebase awareness

See [`references/context-and-codebase-awareness.md`](references/context-and-codebase-awareness.md). 1M-token context windows are now standard for the highest-end model in 4 of the 6 platforms. Cursor's local-Merkle-tree + remote-embedding pipeline keeps code local, sending only embeddings; this is the most-documented privacy-aware indexing approach. GitHub Copilot's server-side semantic indexing is the most-mature server-side approach. Bob's 200K context with auto-condensation at 140K is the smallest in the group — a deliberate choice for legacy-code understanding rather than monorepo refactor.

## Dimension 6: IDE and ecosystem

See [`references/ide-and-ecosystem.md`](references/ide-and-ecosystem.md). GitHub Copilot has the broadest IDE coverage in the market (8+ editors) [15]. Cursor's June 2025 forced migration to OpenVSX is an ongoing pain point — some Microsoft-proprietary extensions remain inaccessible. Bob-IDE imports VS Code, Cursor, and Windsurf settings on first run [27], reducing migration friction.

## Dimension 7: Benchmarks and real-world quality

See [`references/benchmarks-and-real-world-quality.md`](references/benchmarks-and-real-world-quality.md). On SWE-bench Verified (the dominant published benchmark), **Claude Opus 4.7 leads at 87.6%** [32]; GPT-5.3 Codex at 85.0%; Gemini 3 not listed. **But SWE-bench Verified is being abandoned** by OpenAI due to contamination evidence; SWE-bench Pro shows the same Opus 4.5 dropping from 80.9% Verified to 45.9% Pro — a 35-point gap [33]. Gemini does dominate LiveCodeBench (algorithmic coding) — it depends what "coding quality" you measure. Real-world quality signals: Gemini 2.5 Pro hallucinated through 39 turns and 693 lines on a 2-line bug [36]; Cursor 2.1.50 had multiple confirmed regressions including silent file emptying [11]. METR's RCT measured developers as 19% slower with AI tools while perceiving themselves 20% faster [34]; GitClear's repo analysis shows code duplication rising 8.3% → 12.3% [35].

## Dimension 8: Privacy and data handling

See [`references/privacy-and-data-handling.md`](references/privacy-and-data-handling.md). The biggest cross-platform shift in 2025-2026 is the convergence of individual paid tiers toward "we use your data for training by default unless you opt out": Anthropic effective Aug 28 2025 [3], GitHub Copilot effective April 24 2026 [14], Gemini Code Assist Individual already does so on free tier [20]. **Business / Enterprise / API tiers are excluded from training** on all three. The buying-decision implication: an individual tier and a Business tier on the same platform now have materially different privacy postures. Cursor's Privacy Mode is a true ZDR mode when manually enabled [9]. IBM Bob has the strongest data-residency story (customer-cloud deployment) but the weakest surfaced "code not for training" pledge.

## Cross-cutting observations

1. **Convergence at the model layer; differentiation at the surface layer.** With 4 of 6 platforms exposing Claude Opus and most exposing Gemini and GPT, "which model" is no longer the differentiator. The IDE / agent / context-handling layer is.

2. **MCP is the new ecosystem currency.** All six platforms support MCP. Built-in MCP servers (GitHub Copilot ships GitHub + Playwright; Windsurf ships GitHub + Slack + Stripe + Figma + databases) reduce setup friction and may become a soft lock-in mechanism. Claude Code's Skills are an alternative orthogonal mechanism that uses ~30-50 tokens instead of MCP's ~55K for a typical 5-server setup [6].

3. **Pricing is unstable.** This research period saw a pricing apology (Cursor July 2025 [10]), a silent pricing flip-flop (Anthropic April 22, 2026 [5]), a signup pause (GitHub Copilot April 20, 2026 [12][13]), and quota cuts (Antigravity March 2026 [19]). Any specific dollar figure in this comparison is a snapshot, not a commitment.

4. **The training-data default has flipped.** Two of the three platforms make this explicit: GitHub Copilot Free/Pro/Pro+ now uses interaction data for training by default (effective April 24, 2026) [14], and Gemini Code Assist Individual collects prompts/code for training with opt-out available [20]. Anthropic's August 2025 consumer terms update presents users with a choice on training data use [3]; whether the default for new accounts is opt-in or opt-out depends on signup-flow framing not surfaced in the news post itself. Across all three, **Business / Enterprise / API tiers are excluded from training**. Privacy now scales with tier, not just with vendor.

5. **Independent productivity evidence is weaker than vendor evidence.** GitHub's controlled study claims 55% faster [16]; METR's RCT measures 19% slower [34]; GitClear's repo data shows declining refactoring rates [35]; the Pragmatic Engineer 2026 survey shows enthusiastic adoption [37]. The space is enthusiastic about itself; rigorous independent measurement is sparse.

## Fit-by-workflow guide

The user lens is "individual / small team picking a tool." Here's the decision tree:

**If you live in the terminal:** Claude Code on Pro $20/mo is the canonical fit — the CLI is the canonical surface and Opus 4.7 leads SWE-bench Verified [1][2][32]. Gemini CLI (free tier) is the open-source-and-no-cost alternative, with the caveat of Flash-only on free API key.

**If you want a single visual IDE and don't mind a fork:** Cursor on Pro $20/mo is the most-developed fork-IDE [7]. Composer 2 is now the cheapest-per-token frontier coder ($0.50/M input [8]). Watch for the Cursor 2.1.50-style regressions and use Privacy Mode if data handling matters [9][11].

**If you live in JetBrains or Visual Studio:** GitHub Copilot is the only platform with first-party support [15]. **Caveat: Pro/Pro+ signups are paused as of April 20, 2026** — if you don't already have a Pro subscription, only Free, Business, or Enterprise can be set up new today [12][13][38]. Free is now training-data-by-default [14].

**If you already pay for Google AI Pro:** Antigravity is currently the cheapest path to Claude Opus 4.6 specifically [19] — though Pro users have reported 7-10 day lockouts in practice. Gemini Code Assist + Gemini CLI share the same Google AI subscription, so you get a multi-surface family for one $19.99 fee.

**If you want an autonomous "delegate it and walk away" model:** Windsurf Max with embedded Devin Cloud sessions [21][22][39] is the strongest hybrid local-plan + cloud-execute pattern. GitHub Copilot Coding Agent (assign issue → get PR) is the strongest cloud-only model but pricing requires Pro+ ($39/mo) which isn't currently signup-able [12].

**If your stack is RPG / COBOL / IBM i:** IBM Bob is purpose-built for legacy modernization, with RPG, CL, SQL, COBOL, Java, and Python support [26]. Native IBM i connection is missing in 1.0 but planned for Q2 2026 [28]. Verify the security patches from PromptArmor's January 2026 disclosures are remediated before deploying [30].

**If you want to keep $20/month total spend across the team:** Two paths. (a) **Antigravity preview free tier** during preview, with reliability tradeoffs [19]; (b) **Gemini Code Assist Individual free tier** at 1,000 requests/user/day [17] — be aware of training-data default. Free GitHub Copilot is also still signup-able but the privacy cost is now meaningful [14].

## Limitations and time-decay

- **Time-stamped data:** Every numeric claim in this document is dated to research conducted April 26, 2026. The 4 events between April 15-24, 2026 ([5][14][22][13]) demonstrate how fast pricing and policy can change. Re-verify before relying on specific dollar figures or model versions.
- **Sources reachable in-session:** ~30 URLs were directly fetched and verified; remainder of citations rely on Discovery agent search-result extraction. Specific known gaps: the SWE-bench leaderboard live page [31] returned only loading scaffolding; the IBM Project Bob official announcement [agent research] returned 403; the OpenAI SWE-bench retirement post returned 403; Antigravity's pricing page returned only a title.
- **Counter-perspectives are unevenly distributed.** Cursor (pricing controversy [10], regressions [11]), Claude Code (pricing flip-flop [5]), and GitHub Copilot (Pro pause + privacy reversal [13][14]) have rich counter-perspective evidence. IBM Bob has thinner critical literature beyond the security disclosure [30] and post-GA "missing IBM i connection" complaint [28] — partly because Bob is too new for sustained critique. Windsurf's critique is dominated by ownership-instability concerns [23] rather than product-quality concerns. Antigravity's critique is rate-limit reliability [19].
- **The METR study sample size is small** (n=16) [34]. Vendors will (correctly) note this is statistically borderline. The finding is directional, not generalizable.
- **GitHub's productivity study has industry-citation conflict** [16] — n=95 controlled task is far from real-world; the BlueOptima counter-analysis (referenced in counter-perspective research) reports 4% productivity gain on 218,000 real developers via commit data, vs the 55% controlled-task figure.
- **Vendor benchmarks are vendor benchmarks.** Cursor's CursorBench [8], Windsurf's SWE-1.5/1.6 figures [24], IBM's "45% productivity" claim [agent research, IBM Think blog] are all self-reported and unaudited.
- **One discrepancy left for the reader:** the IT Jungle GA article [26] characterizes Bob as a "VS Code plug-in" while the December first-look [27] explicitly calls it "a full fork of VS Code." This deliverable trusts [27] as the more architectural source. A buyer should verify directly at install time.

## Reflection

This deliverable is written through an individual / small-team lens. A buyer should verify three things before committing:

1. **Whether the price is still the price.** All listed prices were current April 26, 2026; four material pricing/policy events fired in the previous 11 days.
2. **Whether the security and privacy disclosures match the buyer's tolerance.** IBM Bob has unresolved security disclosure history [30]; three platforms (Anthropic, GitHub, Google) flipped training-data defaults to opt-in within the last 8 months [3][14][20].
3. **Whether the platform is doing what its marketing says, today.** Cursor 2.1.50 [11] and Gemini's 39-turn hallucination [36] are reminders that vendor claims and shipped behavior diverge.

The honest framing is that no single platform "wins" this comparison. The answer depends on workflow (terminal vs IDE), existing subscriptions (Anthropic / Google / GitHub / Cognition), and tolerance for billing surprises. The fit-by-workflow guide above captures the patterns I'd recommend.
